transcript.heading: News Report One (British Male)
paras: A new study has found that reading for just 20 minutes a day can significantly reduce stress levels and improve overall mental health, according to researchers at the University of Sussex. The study measured the stress levels of participants before and after different relaxing activities, including reading, listening to music, going for a walk, and drinking tea. They found that reading was the most effective activity for reducing stress, lowering heart rate and muscle tension by up to 68 percent within just six minutes of starting to read. Researchers say that reading works so well because it requires concentration, which distracts the mind from worrying thoughts and daily stresses, and it also relaxes the body because you're sitting still and breathing more slowly. The type of reading didn't matter as much as just reading something you enjoy—whether it's a novel, a magazine, or an article online, as long as it engages your attention. However, researchers noted that reading on screens like phones or tablets was slightly less effective than reading physical books, possibly because notifications and other distractions on devices make it harder to fully immerse yourself. They recommend making reading a daily habit, even if it's just for a short time, as a simple and effective way to manage stress.

transcript.heading: News Report Two (American Female)
paras: The city of Portland, Oregon has become the first major city in the United States to ban all new single-use plastic items, including plastic utensils, straws, stirrers, and foam food containers, in an effort to reduce plastic waste and pollution. The ban, which will go into effect next year, applies to all restaurants, cafes, food trucks, and grocery stores in the city. Businesses that violate the ban will face fines starting at $100 for the first offense and increasing for repeated violations. The city says that single-use plastics make up a significant portion of the waste that ends up in landfills, rivers, and oceans, and that they can take hundreds of years to break down. They also harm wildlife, which can mistake plastic for food or become entangled in it. The ban has been supported by environmental groups, who say it's an important step toward reducing plastic pollution. Some business owners, however, have expressed concerns that the ban will increase their costs, since paper and compostable alternatives are more expensive than plastic. The city says it will provide support and resources to help small businesses make the transition, and that the long-term environmental benefits are worth the short-term costs.

transcript.heading: News Report Three (American Male)
paras: Scientists at Stanford University have developed a new type of flexible, wearable battery that can be stretched, bent, and even washed without losing its ability to hold a charge, opening up new possibilities for wearable electronics and smart clothing. Traditional batteries are rigid and bulky, which limits how they can be used in wearable devices. The new battery is made from a special stretchable polymer material that contains conductive silver nanowires, and it can be stretched up to twice its original size without breaking or losing performance. It's also waterproof and can survive being washed in a washing machine, which is important for clothing-integrated electronics. Researchers say the battery could be used in all kinds of wearable devices, from smart watches and fitness trackers that are more comfortable to wear, to medical sensors that can be worn directly on the skin, to clothing with built-in electronics like heated jackets or shirts that monitor your health. The battery is still in the early stages of development, and researchers are working on increasing its energy storage capacity and lowering production costs before it can be brought to market. But they say the technology could revolutionize wearable electronics within the next decade.

transcript.heading: Conversation One (American Male + American Female)
paras: Man (Ryan): Hey Emma, I heard you're planning a trip to Japan next summer. That's so exciting!

Woman (Emma): Yeah, I'm really excited! I've wanted to go to Japan for years, and I finally saved up enough money. But I'm also kind of overwhelmed—there's so much to plan and I don't even know where to start.
Man: Oh, I've been to Japan twice! I can give you some tips if you want.
Woman: Really? That would be amazing! Thank you so much. First of all, how long should I go for? I was thinking two weeks, but I don't know if that's enough or too much.
Man: Two weeks is perfect for a first trip. You can see Tokyo, Kyoto, Osaka, and maybe a day trip or two. Any longer and you might get tired, any shorter and you'll feel rushed.
Woman: Good, that's what I was thinking. What cities should I definitely visit?

Man: Well, Tokyo is a must—it's this amazing, huge, futuristic city with so much to do. You need at least three or four days there just to scratch the surface. Then you should definitely go to Kyoto—it's the old capital, full of temples, shrines, and traditional Japanese culture. It's like stepping back in time compared to Tokyo. Osaka is also great—it's more laid-back, has amazing food, and it's a good base for day trips to places like Nara, where you can see the deer.
Woman: That sounds perfect. What about transportation? How do you get around between cities?

Man: The Shinkansen—the bullet train—is the best way. It's super fast, super comfortable, and always on time. It's a little expensive, but it's worth it. You can also buy a Japan Rail Pass before you go, which gives you unlimited rides on most trains for a set price. That can save you a lot of money if you're traveling between cities a lot.
Woman: Good to know. What about food? I've heard Japanese food is amazing, but I'm a vegetarian. Will I have trouble finding things to eat?

Man: Hmm, that's a good question. Japanese cuisine uses a lot of fish and meat, and even things that seem vegetarian often have fish sauce or bonito flakes in them. But it's definitely doable. There are vegetarian restaurants in the bigger cities, especially Tokyo and Kyoto, and Buddhist temples often have amazing vegetarian meals called shojin ryori. You just have to do a little research and plan ahead. And convenience stores actually have a lot of vegetarian options too—onigiri with pickled plum, edamame, salads, things like that.
Woman: That's a relief. I was worried I'd have to live on rice the whole time. What about the language barrier? I don't speak any Japanese. Will that be a problem?

Man: It's really not as bad as you might think. In the big cities and tourist areas, a lot of people speak at least a little English, and most signs have English translations. And even when people don't speak English, they're usually really helpful and will try to communicate with gestures or translation apps. You should download a translation app before you go, and maybe learn a few basic phrases like hello, thank you, and excuse me. People really appreciate it when you make an effort.
Woman: That's good to hear. Is there anything else I should know before I go?

Man: Oh, lots of things! But the main thing is just to be open-minded and respectful of the culture. Japan is a very polite, orderly society, and there are a lot of little customs—like taking off your shoes indoors, not tipping, being quiet on trains. But people are very forgiving of tourists who make honest mistakes. Just be polite and you'll be fine.
Woman: Thanks so much for all the advice, Ryan. You've been a huge help. I'm even more excited now!
Man: No problem! You're going to have an amazing time. Let me know if you have more questions as you plan.

transcript.heading: Conversation Two (British Female + British Male)
paras: Woman (Olivia): Hey Liam, what are you working on? You've been staring at your computer screen for hours.
Man (Liam): Oh, hey Olivia. I'm trying to write my personal statement for my university application. It's due next week and I have no idea what to write. I'm so stuck.
Woman: Ugh, I remember how stressful that was. What are you applying to study again?

Man: Computer science. I want to study artificial intelligence and machine learning. But how do I write a personal statement that makes me stand out from all the other applicants? Everyone applying probably likes computers and is good at math.

Woman: Well, that's true, but everyone has different experiences and reasons for wanting to study it. The point of a personal statement is to show who you are as a person, not just list your grades. What made you interested in AI in the first place?

Man: Hmm, I guess it started when I was a kid and I was really into robots and science fiction. But then in high school, I took a programming class and I realized I could actually build things that were kind of intelligent. Last year, I built a little program that could recognize different types of flowers from photos, and it actually worked pretty well. That's when I knew I wanted to study this seriously.

Woman: That's perfect! You should definitely write about that. Admissions officers love to hear about specific projects and experiences that show your passion and initiative. It's way more interesting than just saying "I'm interested in AI."
Man: Yeah, but what if my project is too simple? I'm sure other applicants have done way more impressive things.

Woman: It doesn't matter how impressive it is—what matters is that you did it on your own, that you were curious and motivated enough to teach yourself and build something. That shows initiative and passion, which is exactly what universities are looking for. Grades are important, but they want to see that you actually care about the subject and that you'll be a good student who contributes to the department.
Man: I guess that makes sense. What else should I include?

Woman: You should also talk about why you want to study at that particular university. Do they have specific courses or research programs that you're interested in? Mention those—it shows you've done your research and you're genuinely interested in their program, not just any program.
Man: Yeah, there are a few professors whose research I find really interesting. Should I mention them by name?
Woman: Absolutely! That shows you've really looked into the program. But don't just name-drop—explain why their work interests you and how it relates to your own goals.
Man: Okay, that's helpful. What about structure? How should I organize it?

Woman: Start with a hook—something interesting that grabs the reader's attention, like the story of your flower recognition project. Then explain how you got interested in the subject, what experiences you've had that prepared you, why you want to study at their university specifically, and what your goals are for the future. End with a strong conclusion that ties it all together.
Man: That makes sense. But I'm worried it will sound cheesy or generic.

Woman: Just be honest and write in your own voice. Don't try to sound like someone you're not, and don't use big words you wouldn't normally use. Admissions officers read hundreds of these—they can tell when someone is being fake. The best personal statements are the ones that feel genuine and give you a real sense of who the person is.
Man: Thanks, Olivia. That's really helpful. I feel a little less stuck now.
Woman: No problem! And if you want, I can read it over when you're done and give you feedback. I've read a lot of personal statements, so I know what works and what doesn't.
Man: That would be amazing! Thank you so much.

transcript.heading: Passage One (British Male)
paras: The Great Wall of China is one of the most famous and impressive structures in the world, but there are many misconceptions about it. Contrary to popular belief, the Great Wall is not a single, continuous wall that was built all at once by one emperor—it's actually a series of walls and fortifications built by different dynasties over thousands of years, and much of it is in ruins today.

The earliest parts of the Great Wall were built as early as the 7th century BC by various states during the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods, to protect against invasions from neighboring states and nomadic tribes. When Qin Shi Huang unified China in 221 BC and became the first emperor, he ordered the connection and extension of these existing walls to create a unified defense system against the Xiongnu people from the north. This was the first "Great Wall," but very little of the Qin wall remains today.

Over the centuries, subsequent dynasties continued to build, rebuild, and extend the wall. The most famous and best-preserved sections of the Great Wall that people visit today were built during the Ming Dynasty, from the 14th to the 17th centuries. The Ming Wall is the most extensive and well-constructed version, made of brick and stone instead of the earlier rammed earth, and it includes watchtowers, barracks, and signal towers.

Another common myth is that the Great Wall is visible from space with the naked eye. In reality, this is not true—the wall is only about 6 to 7 meters wide, which is too narrow to be seen from space without magnification. Astronauts have confirmed that you can't see the Great Wall from the moon, and it's very difficult to see even from low Earth orbit. This myth has been around for hundreds of years, long before space travel was even possible, and it persists despite being debunked.

At its peak during the Ming Dynasty, the Great Wall stretched for over 8,850 kilometers, including all its branches and extensions. But today, much of the wall has been destroyed by natural erosion, human development, and theft of bricks for building materials. Some sections have been restored for tourism, but many remote sections are in poor condition or have disappeared entirely.

Despite the myths and misconceptions, the Great Wall remains an incredible feat of engineering and a powerful symbol of Chinese history and civilization. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the most popular tourist attractions in the world, drawing millions of visitors every year.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (American Female)
paras: The science of sleep has advanced dramatically in recent decades, and we now know that sleep is far more important and complex than people used to think. Getting enough good quality sleep is essential for physical health, mental health, cognitive function, and overall well-being, yet millions of people around the world don't get enough sleep.

During sleep, your body doesn't just shut down—it's actively working to repair cells, regulate hormones, consolidate memories, and process emotions. There are several stages of sleep that you cycle through multiple times each night, including light sleep, deep sleep, and REM (rapid eye movement) sleep, and each stage serves different important functions.

Deep sleep is when your body repairs itself—growth hormone is released, tissue is repaired, and the immune system is strengthened. It's also when memories are transferred from short-term to long-term storage. REM sleep, on the other hand, is when most dreaming occurs, and it's important for emotional processing, learning, and creativity. During REM sleep, your brain is almost as active as when you're awake, but your body is temporarily paralyzed so you don't act out your dreams.

Not getting enough sleep has serious consequences. In the short term, sleep deprivation causes fatigue, difficulty concentrating, memory problems, mood swings, and reduced reaction time. It also impairs judgment and decision-making, which is why sleep deprivation is a major cause of car accidents and workplace errors. In the long term, chronic sleep deprivation increases the risk of many serious health problems, including heart disease, diabetes, obesity, depression, and even dementia.

Despite all this, many people treat sleep as a luxury or something they can skimp on when they're busy. They stay up late working, studying, or scrolling through their phones, thinking they can just catch up on sleep on the weekends. But you can't really "catch up" on sleep—while sleeping in on weekends might help you feel a little better, it doesn't fully reverse the effects of sleep deprivation during the week, and it can even disrupt your circadian rhythm further.

Experts recommend that adults get between 7 and 9 hours of sleep per night, and that they maintain a consistent sleep schedule even on weekends. Good sleep hygiene—like having a regular bedtime routine, keeping your bedroom dark and cool, avoiding caffeine and screens before bed, and getting regular exercise—can help improve the quality of your sleep.

Sleep is not a waste of time—it's essential for your brain and body to function properly. Prioritizing sleep is one of the best things you can do for your health, your productivity, and your happiness.

transcript.heading: Passage Three (American Male)
paras: The history of video games is a story of rapid technological innovation and cultural change, from simple arcade games in the 1970s to the immersive, realistic games of today. In just a few decades, video games have grown from a niche hobby into one of the largest forms of entertainment in the world, bigger than the movie and music industries combined.

The first video games were developed in the 1950s and 1960s as experiments in university computer labs, but they weren't available to the general public. The first commercially successful video game was Pong, a simple table tennis game released by Atari in 1972. Pong was a huge hit, and it launched the arcade game industry, with arcades popping up in malls and shopping centers around the world.

The 1980s saw the rise of home video game consoles, starting with the Atari 2600 and later the Nintendo Entertainment System, which brought video games into people's living rooms. Classic games like Super Mario Bros., The Legend of Zelda, and Pac-Man became cultural icons, and video games became a mainstream form of entertainment for children and teenagers.

The 1990s brought major advances in graphics and gameplay, with the transition from 2D to 3D graphics and the rise of CD-ROMs that allowed for much larger games with voice acting and music. Consoles like the Sony PlayStation and Nintendo 64 introduced millions of people to 3D gaming, and PC gaming also grew in popularity with the rise of first-person shooters and real-time strategy games.

The 2000s and 2010s saw even more changes. Online gaming became mainstream, allowing people to play with friends and strangers from all over the world. Mobile gaming exploded with the rise of smartphones, making games accessible to almost everyone and introducing whole new audiences to gaming. Indie games—made by small teams or even individual developers without big studio backing—became more popular and influential, thanks to digital distribution platforms that made it easy for small developers to reach audiences.

Today, video games are a global phenomenon with billions of players. They're not just for kids anymore—the average age of a gamer is in their 30s, and games are played by people of all ages, genders, and backgrounds. Esports—competitive video gaming—has become a huge industry with professional players, huge prize pools, and millions of viewers. Virtual reality and augmented reality are pushing the boundaries of what games can be, making them more immersive than ever.

While video games have sometimes been criticized for being violent or addictive, research has shown that they can also have benefits, like improving problem-solving skills, hand-eye coordination, and even social skills when played with others. Like any form of entertainment, moderation is key, but there's no denying that video games have become an important part of modern culture and technology.
